concepts.reference: Analytical warehouses such as Snowflake, BigQuery and Redshift typically store data by column. Queries read only the columns they need, similar values compress well, and scans parallelize across nodes. Single-row updates are comparatively expensive.
concepts.check: Why is columnar storage efficient for summing one column over millions of rows?
concepts.bridge: Row storage keeps each record together; columnar storage keeps each column's values together.

concepts.name: Slowly changing dimensions
concepts.reference: Dimension attributes such as a customer's region change over time. Type 1 overwrites the value and loses history. Type 2 adds a new row with effective dates, so past facts keep pointing to the attribute values that were true when they happened.
concepts.check: Which approach keeps last year's sales attributed to a customer's old region?
concepts.bridge: A dimension attribute is descriptive context such as region, product category or customer segment.

background: Applications store data for running the business, one transaction at a time. Questions about trends across months, products and regions need data combined and shaped differently.
practice: Analytics teams load data into warehouses such as Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift or Databricks and model it with tools like dbt. Business intelligence tools such as Power BI and Tableau work best on star schemas. Document each table's grain and keep dimension history where reports need it.

title: Event streaming with Kafka
prompt: Explain how Kafka stores and delivers events, and what guarantees a consumer can rely on.
compare: Compare event streaming with nightly batch processing for detecting fraudulent transactions.
core: Kafka is a distributed log. Producers append events to topics, which are split into partitions. Consumers read events in order within each partition and track their position with offsets, so events can be processed continuously and replayed.
example: A payment service publishes each transaction to a topic keyed by account ID. All events for one account land in the same partition, so a fraud consumer sees them in order. A consumer group spreads partitions across instances to share the load.
nuance: Kafka orders events within a partition, not across a whole topic. Default delivery is at least once, so consumers must tolerate duplicates. Exactly-once semantics apply to specific Kafka read-process-write patterns, not automatically to external side effects like sending an email.

concepts.name: Topics, partitions and offsets
concepts.reference: A topic is a named stream of events stored as an append-only log. It is divided into partitions that can live on different brokers and are replicated for fault tolerance. Each event in a partition has an increasing offset. Events are retained for a configured time or size, not deleted when read.
concepts.check: Why can a new consumer replay last week's events?
concepts.bridge: A log is an ordered sequence of records that only grows at the end.

concepts.name: Keys and ordering
concepts.reference: Producers can attach a key, and events with the same key go to the same partition by default. Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition. Choosing the key determines which events stay ordered relative to each other and how evenly load spreads.
concepts.check: What key would keep all updates for one order in sequence?
concepts.bridge: A partition is processed sequentially, so it is the unit of both ordering and parallelism.

concepts.name: Consumer groups
concepts.reference: Consumers in the same group divide a topic's partitions so each partition is read by one member at a time. Adding consumers increases parallelism up to the partition count. When members join or fail, the group rebalances partitions. Separate groups each receive all events independently.
concepts.check: Why does adding a tenth consumer to a topic with eight partitions not help?
concepts.bridge: A consumer group is a set of instances sharing the work of reading one subscription.

concepts.name: Delivery semantics
concepts.reference: If a consumer commits offsets after processing, a crash causes reprocessing and duplicates: at least once. Committing before processing risks losing events: at most once. Kafka transactions and idempotent producers support exactly-once processing within Kafka; external effects still need idempotent handling.
concepts.check: How would you make a consumer safe when it may see the same payment event twice?
concepts.bridge: Committing an offset records that a consumer has finished with events up to that position.

background: Some data is most useful the moment it happens, such as payments, sensor readings or clicks. Streaming platforms let many systems react to the same events continuously instead of waiting for a nightly batch.
practice: Teams use Kafka, or managed services such as Confluent Cloud and Amazon MSK, to connect microservices and feed real-time pipelines. Design keys for ordering, size partitions for throughput, monitor consumer lag, and make consumers idempotent. A schema registry helps producers and consumers agree on event formats.

title: Data quality and validation
prompt: How would you make sure the data feeding a dashboard or model is trustworthy?
compare: Compare validating data at ingestion with validating it after it reaches the warehouse.
core: Data quality means data is accurate, complete, consistent, timely and valid for its intended use. Validation checks encode those expectations as automated tests so problems are caught before people or models rely on bad data.
example: A pipeline loading patient survey responses checks that each response ID is unique, scores are between 0 and 10, required fields are present, and today's file arrived. Rows that fail go to a quarantine table, and the team is alerted if the failure rate spikes.
nuance: Passing checks shows data meets the written expectations, not that it is correct. Overly strict checks that block everything get disabled; overly loose ones miss real problems. Some issues, like a source silently changing a unit, need distribution and anomaly checks rather than simple rules.

concepts.name: Quality dimensions
concepts.reference: Common dimensions include completeness (required values present), validity (values match types, formats and ranges), uniqueness (no unintended duplicates), consistency (values agree across tables), accuracy (values reflect reality) and timeliness (data is fresh enough).
concepts.check: Which dimension fails when the same order is loaded twice?
concepts.bridge: Quality depends on use: data fresh enough for a monthly report may be too stale for an alert.

concepts.name: Automated checks
concepts.reference: Tests assert expectations such as not-null, accepted values, ranges, referential integrity, row-count changes and freshness. Tools like dbt tests and Great Expectations run them in the pipeline. Statistical checks flag unusual shifts in distributions or volumes.
concepts.check: Why might a sudden 40 percent drop in row count deserve an alert even if every row is valid?
concepts.bridge: A check turns an expectation about data into a test that passes or fails automatically.

concepts.name: Schemas and data contracts
concepts.reference: A data contract is an agreed definition between producer and consumer of a dataset's schema, meanings and guarantees. Validating against it at the boundary catches breaking changes, such as a renamed field or changed unit, before downstream jobs consume them.
concepts.check: Who should be notified when a source team plans to change a field's type?
concepts.bridge: A producer creates data; consumers are the pipelines, reports or models that depend on it.

concepts.name: Handling bad data
concepts.reference: Options include failing the pipeline, quarantining invalid rows for review, or loading with flags. Choose based on impact: blocking protects consumers but delays data; quarantine keeps good data flowing. Record lineage so you can trace an issue to its source and affected outputs.
concepts.check: When would you stop the whole pipeline instead of quarantining rows?
concepts.bridge: Lineage records where data came from and which downstream tables and reports use it.

background: Reports, models and decisions are only as good as their input data. Sources change, files arrive late and bugs introduce duplicates, often without any error message.
practice: Data teams add tests to pipelines with dbt, Great Expectations or custom SQL, monitor freshness and volume, and alert owners when checks fail. In evaluation or research data, curation and validation are part of the work, and documenting known limitations is as important as fixing errors.

title: Distributed processing with Spark
prompt: Explain how Apache Spark processes a large dataset across a cluster, and what makes a Spark job slow.
compare: Compare processing a dataset with pandas on one machine and with Spark on a cluster.
core: Spark splits data into partitions and processes them in parallel across executors in a cluster. Programs build a plan of transformations lazily; an action triggers execution, and the optimizer turns the plan into stages of tasks.
example: A job reads a year of event logs, filters to one product, and counts events per user. The filter runs independently on each partition. Counting per user requires a shuffle so that all events for one user meet on the same executor before the final count.
nuance: Spark is not automatically faster than a single machine; small data often runs quicker in pandas or SQL. Shuffles, skewed keys and collecting large results to the driver are common bottlenecks. Calling an action repeatedly recomputes the plan unless data is cached.

concepts.name: Transformations and actions
concepts.reference: Transformations such as filter, select and join describe a new dataset without computing it. Actions such as count, collect and write trigger execution. Laziness lets Spark's Catalyst optimizer combine steps, push filters toward the data source and prune unused columns.
concepts.check: Why might a long chain of transformations run in under a second until you call count?
concepts.bridge: Lazy evaluation means recording what to compute and deferring the work until a result is needed.

concepts.name: Partitions and parallelism
concepts.reference: A DataFrame is divided into partitions, and each task processes one partition on an executor. The number and size of partitions determine parallelism. Too few partitions underuse the cluster; too many create scheduling overhead and tiny files.
concepts.check: What happens if a large dataset has only two partitions on a 50-core cluster?
concepts.bridge: The driver plans the job; executors are worker processes that run tasks on partitions.

concepts.name: Shuffles and skew
concepts.reference: Wide operations such as groupBy, join and distinct require redistributing rows by key across the network, called a shuffle. Shuffles are expensive and define stage boundaries. Skew, where one key has far more rows, leaves one task running long after others finish. Broadcast joins avoid shuffling a small table.
concepts.check: Why would a join with a small lookup table benefit from broadcasting it?
concepts.bridge: Narrow operations work within one partition; wide operations need data from many partitions.

concepts.name: DataFrames and Spark SQL
concepts.reference: DataFrames are distributed tables with a schema, queried through an API or Spark SQL, and they let the optimizer plan efficiently. Python UDFs can block optimizations and add serialization cost; built-in functions are usually faster. Platforms such as Databricks run Spark with managed clusters and Delta Lake tables.
concepts.check: Why prefer a built-in Spark function over a Python UDF for string cleanup?
concepts.bridge: PySpark is Spark's Python interface; the computation still runs in Spark's engine on the cluster.

sources.title: Apache Spark: SQL, DataFrames and Datasets guide

background: Some datasets are too large for one computer's memory or would take hours to process on one core. Distributed engines split the work across many machines while presenting a familiar table-like interface.
practice: Data engineers use PySpark and Spark SQL on Databricks, EMR or similar platforms for large ETL jobs and feature pipelines. Read the Spark UI to find slow stages, reduce shuffles, handle skewed keys, write partitioned columnar files such as Parquet, and avoid collecting large results to the driver.

title: A/B testing and statistical significance
prompt: Explain how an A/B test shows whether a change actually improved a metric.
compare: Compare a randomized A/B test with comparing metrics before and after a launch.
core: An A/B test randomly assigns users to a control or a variant and compares a predefined metric. Randomization makes the groups comparable, so a difference larger than expected from chance can be attributed to the change.
example: A team tests a new onboarding screen. Half of new users see it at random. After reaching the sample size planned in advance, the variant's completion rate is 3 points higher with a confidence interval that excludes zero, so the team ships it.
nuance: A p-value below 0.05 is not the probability the change works, and statistical significance is not practical importance. Repeatedly peeking and stopping when results look good inflates false positives. Testing many metrics or segments produces some significant results by chance.

concepts.name: Randomization and control
concepts.reference: Random assignment balances known and unknown differences between groups on average, so the control group shows what would have happened without the change. Assignment should be at a stable unit, such as user, and consistent across visits. Before-after comparisons are confounded by seasonality and other changes.
concepts.check: Why is comparing this week's signups with last week's weaker evidence than a randomized test?
concepts.bridge: The control group keeps the current experience; the variant receives the change being tested.

concepts.name: Hypothesis tests and p-values
concepts.reference: The null hypothesis says the change has no effect. A p-value is the probability of observing a difference at least as extreme as the one seen if the null were true. A confidence interval gives a range of effect sizes consistent with the data.
concepts.check: What does a p-value of 0.03 actually tell you?
concepts.bridge: Random variation means two identical groups will rarely produce exactly the same metric.

concepts.name: Power and sample size
concepts.reference: Power is the probability of detecting a true effect of a given size. It increases with sample size and effect size and decreases with metric variance. Teams choose a minimum detectable effect and compute the needed sample size before starting.
concepts.check: Why might a test with too few users fail to detect a real improvement?
concepts.bridge: Underpowered tests often return inconclusive results, which is not the same as proving no effect.

concepts.name: Peeking and multiple comparisons
concepts.reference: Checking results repeatedly and stopping at the first significant moment raises the false-positive rate unless a sequential method is used. Testing many metrics or segments also raises it; predefine a primary metric and correct for multiple comparisons. Guardrail metrics watch for harm elsewhere.
concepts.check: Why should the primary metric be chosen before the test starts?
concepts.bridge: A false positive is concluding a change works when the observed difference was chance.

sources.title: Kohavi et al.: Controlled experiments on the web (Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery)

background: Teams constantly change products and want to know whether a change helped. Metrics fluctuate for many reasons, so a careful experiment separates the change's effect from noise and outside events.
practice: Product and data science teams run experiments through feature-flag platforms or in-house tools and analyze them in SQL or Python. A good analysis states the hypothesis, primary metric, sample size and duration in advance, reports effect sizes with intervals, and checks guardrail metrics before shipping.

title: Designing metrics and dashboards
prompt: How would you design a dashboard that helps a team make better decisions?
compare: Compare a leading indicator with a lagging indicator for a patient-engagement app.
core: A metric is a precisely defined measurement that represents something a team cares about. A good dashboard presents a small number of trustworthy metrics, chosen for a specific audience and decision, with enough context to interpret changes.
example: For a health-coaching app, the team defines weekly active users as users who log at least one goal in a Monday-to-Sunday week. The dashboard shows that trend, goal completion rate and a retention curve, each with its definition and a data-freshness note.
nuance: Averages can hide distributions, ratios can mislead when the denominator changes, and totals can grow while each user does less. A metric that becomes a target can be gamed. More charts usually make a dashboard harder to use, not more useful.

concepts.name: Precise metric definitions
concepts.reference: A usable metric specifies its numerator, denominator, time window, filters and data source. Ambiguous names like active user lead to different numbers in different reports. Writing definitions down, ideally in a shared semantic layer, keeps everyone measuring the same thing.
concepts.check: What details must you specify before two teams can agree on an active user count?
concepts.bridge: A numerator is what you count; a denominator is the population you divide by.

concepts.name: Leading and lagging indicators
concepts.reference: Lagging indicators, such as revenue or annual retention, measure outcomes after they happen. Leading indicators, such as week-one activation, change earlier and predict those outcomes. Teams act on leading indicators and confirm with lagging ones, while checking that the predictive link actually holds.
concepts.check: Why would a team watch week-one activation instead of waiting for twelve-month retention?
concepts.bridge: An outcome often takes months to measure, so teams look for earlier signals that move with it.

concepts.name: Aggregation pitfalls
concepts.reference: Means are sensitive to outliers; medians and percentiles describe skewed data better. Aggregating across groups can reverse a trend within each group, known as Simpson's paradox. Small denominators make rates noisy, and changing definitions break comparisons over time.
concepts.check: Why might average session length rise while most users' sessions get shorter?
concepts.bridge: Aggregation summarizes many values into one, which can hide how those values are spread.

concepts.name: Designing for an audience
concepts.reference: Start from the decisions the audience makes and show metrics that inform them. Put the most important numbers first, show trends and comparisons for context, label units and definitions, and note data freshness. Executives may need a few headline metrics; operators need detail they can act on.
concepts.check: What question would you ask a stakeholder before building their dashboard?
concepts.bridge: A dashboard is a tool for a decision, not a place to display every available number.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Tips for designing a great Power BI dashboard
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Simpson's paradox

background: Teams collect far more data than anyone can read. Metrics and dashboards condense it into a few numbers people can track, but only if those numbers are well defined and chosen for real decisions.
practice: Analysts build dashboards in Power BI, Tableau, Looker or code-based tools on top of warehouse tables. Interview stakeholders about decisions first, document every metric definition, validate numbers against a known source, and revisit dashboards that nobody uses.

title: What happens when you load a URL
prompt: Walk through what happens between typing a URL into a browser and seeing the page.
compare: Compare a first visit to a page with a repeat visit. Which steps can be skipped or shortened, and why?
core: Loading a URL resolves the host name to an IP address, opens a connection, usually secures it with TLS, sends an HTTP request, and receives a response. The browser then parses the HTML and fetches further resources such as CSS, scripts and images before rendering the page.
example: Visiting https://example.com/docs: the browser checks its caches, then asks a DNS resolver for the address. It opens a TCP connection to port 443, performs a TLS handshake that verifies the server's certificate, and sends GET /docs. The server returns 200 with HTML, which references a stylesheet and a script that trigger further requests.
nuance: Many steps are often skipped: DNS answers, connections and responses can all be reused or cached. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP rather than TCP. TLS protects data in transit but does not make the site itself trustworthy. A fast server response can still produce a slow page if rendering is blocked by large scripts.

concepts.name: DNS resolution
concepts.reference: DNS translates a host name into IP addresses. The browser and operating system check their caches; otherwise a recursive resolver queries root, top-level domain and authoritative name servers. Answers carry a time-to-live that controls how long they may be cached.
concepts.check: Why might a DNS change take time to reach every user?
concepts.bridge: Computers connect using IP addresses, but people type names. DNS is the lookup system that maps one to the other.

concepts.name: Connection and TLS
concepts.reference: The client opens a transport connection, traditionally TCP, and for HTTPS performs a TLS handshake. TLS negotiates encryption keys and lets the client verify the server's certificate against trusted authorities. Reusing an open connection avoids repeating these round trips.
concepts.check: What does the certificate check protect against, and what does it not prove?
concepts.bridge: Before any page data moves, the two machines must agree to talk and, for HTTPS, agree on how to encrypt the conversation.

concepts.name: HTTP request and response
concepts.reference: The client sends a method, path and headers, plus an optional body. The server replies with a status code, headers and an optional body. Status codes group into success (2xx), redirection (3xx), client errors (4xx) and server errors (5xx).
concepts.check: What does a 301 or 302 response cause the browser to do?
concepts.bridge: HTTP is the message format browsers and servers use. Each request asks for something; each response says what happened and returns content.

concepts.name: Caching and rendering
concepts.reference: Headers such as Cache-Control, ETag and Last-Modified let browsers and intermediaries reuse or revalidate responses. The browser parses HTML into the DOM, applies CSS, runs scripts, computes layout and paints. Render-blocking resources delay what the user first sees.
concepts.check: How can a cached response still require a request to the server?
concepts.bridge: Receiving bytes is not the end. The browser must turn HTML, CSS and scripts into pixels, and caching decides which bytes need fetching at all.

background: Every web request crosses several layers: name lookup, a network connection, encryption, an HTTP exchange and browser rendering. Knowing those layers helps you explain where a slow or failing page is actually stuck.
practice: When debugging a slow page, browser developer tools show timing for DNS, connection, TLS, waiting for the server and downloading. Engineers use that breakdown to decide whether to tune caching headers, reduce redirects, reuse connections or shrink render-blocking scripts. A failing request's status code and headers usually narrow the cause faster than guessing.

title: GraphQL versus REST
prompt: Explain how GraphQL works and when you would choose it over a REST API.
compare: Compare fetching a user with their recent orders through REST endpoints versus a single GraphQL query.
core: GraphQL is a query language and runtime for APIs. A server publishes a typed schema, and clients send queries that name exactly the fields they need. Resolver functions fetch each field's data, often from several underlying services.
example: A mobile screen needs a user's name and the titles of their last three orders. With REST it might call /users/42 and then /users/42/orders, receiving extra fields. With GraphQL it sends one query asking for user(id: 42) { name orders(last: 3) { title } } and receives that shape back.
nuance: GraphQL does not make the backend faster; it moves query flexibility to the client. Naive resolvers can cause N+1 database calls. HTTP caching is harder because most queries are POSTs to one endpoint. Clients can write expensive queries, so servers need depth or cost limits. REST remains simpler for many public and cache-friendly APIs.

concepts.name: Schema and types
concepts.reference: A GraphQL schema defines object types, their fields and the root Query and Mutation types. The server validates every query against the schema before running it. Introspection lets tools discover the schema and generate typed clients.
concepts.check: What does validating a query against the schema catch before any data is fetched?
concepts.bridge: The schema is the API's contract: it lists which objects exist, what fields they have, and what clients may ask for.

concepts.name: Over-fetching and under-fetching
concepts.reference: REST endpoints return fixed response shapes, so clients may receive unused fields (over-fetching) or need extra calls to assemble a view (under-fetching). GraphQL lets the client select fields and nested relations in one request.
concepts.check: Why does under-fetching matter more on a slow mobile network?
concepts.bridge: A REST endpoint decides the response shape. A GraphQL client decides it, within what the schema allows.

concepts.name: Resolvers and the N+1 problem
concepts.reference: Each field has a resolver that produces its value. Resolving a list of items and then a related field per item can trigger one query for the list plus one per item. Batching tools such as DataLoader collect those lookups and issue one combined query.
concepts.check: How does batching change the number of database calls for fifty orders?
concepts.bridge: A resolver is the code behind one field. Flexible queries mean the server cannot always predict how many resolvers will run.

concepts.name: Caching, cost and operations
concepts.reference: Because GraphQL usually uses one endpoint, standard URL-based HTTP caching is less effective; clients often normalize cached objects by ID. Servers should limit query depth or complexity, apply per-field authorization, and monitor slow resolvers.
concepts.check: Why might a public GraphQL API need query cost limits?
concepts.bridge: Flexibility for clients shifts responsibility to the server for protecting performance and data access.

background: Front-end screens often need data from several resources at once. REST exposes resources at separate URLs; GraphQL exposes one typed graph that clients query by field. The choice affects network calls, caching and server complexity.
practice: Teams adopt GraphQL when many clients, such as web and mobile apps, need different views of related data. Engineers watch for N+1 resolvers, add batching, limit query cost and check authorization on each field. Small internal services or cache-heavy public endpoints often stay with REST because it is simpler to cache and operate.

title: Rate limiting
prompt: Explain how you would rate limit an API and what the client should experience when it hits the limit.
compare: Compare a fixed-window counter with a token bucket for limiting requests per user.
core: Rate limiting caps how many requests a client may make in a period. It protects services from overload and abuse and shares capacity fairly. When a limit is exceeded, the server rejects or delays requests, commonly returning HTTP 429 Too Many Requests.
example: An LLM API allows each key 60 requests per minute. A token bucket gives each key 60 tokens that refill at one per second; each request spends one token. A burst of 60 succeeds, the 61st receives 429 with a Retry-After header, and the client waits before retrying.
nuance: Fixed windows allow bursts at window edges. Limits need a sensible key: per user, per API key or per IP, and IP limits can punish many users behind one network. Distributed servers need a shared or approximate counter. Rate limiting does not replace capacity planning or authentication.

concepts.name: Limiting algorithms
concepts.reference: A fixed window counts requests per clock interval and resets. A sliding window smooths edges by considering the recent interval. A token bucket refills tokens at a steady rate up to a capacity, allowing short bursts while enforcing an average rate.
concepts.check: Why can a fixed one-minute window allow nearly double the limit in a short span?
concepts.bridge: Each algorithm answers the same question, whether this request is allowed now, with a different balance of simplicity, accuracy and burst tolerance.

concepts.name: Choosing what to limit
concepts.reference: Limits are tracked per key, such as an API key, user ID, IP address or endpoint. Different operations can have different limits; expensive endpoints often get stricter ones. The key determines fairness and who is affected when a limit triggers.
concepts.check: What problem appears if an API limits only by IP address?
concepts.bridge: A rate limit is always a limit for someone. Choosing that someone decides whose traffic gets blocked.

concepts.name: 429 responses and retries
concepts.reference: HTTP 429 indicates too many requests. A Retry-After header can tell the client how long to wait. Well-behaved clients back off, often exponentially with jitter, instead of retrying immediately and adding load.
concepts.check: Why does adding random jitter to retries help a struggling service?
concepts.bridge: A rejected request is only useful if the client understands it and slows down rather than hammering the server again.

concepts.name: Distributed enforcement
concepts.reference: With many application servers, a per-process counter lets clients exceed the global limit. Shared stores such as Redis provide atomic counters, at the cost of an extra network hop. Some systems accept approximate local limits for speed.
concepts.check: What is the trade-off between a shared counter and per-server limits?
concepts.bridge: Load balancers spread one client's requests across servers, so each server sees only part of the traffic.

background: Any public API or shared model server has finite capacity. Without limits, one buggy script or aggressive client can slow or crash the service for everyone else.
practice: Engineers place rate limiting at an API gateway, reverse proxy or application middleware, keyed by API key or user. They return 429 with Retry-After, document limits, and expose remaining quota in headers. Clients calling third-party APIs such as LLM providers implement exponential backoff with jitter and queue work rather than failing outright.

title: Streaming responses: SSE and WebSockets
prompt: Explain how a chat app can stream an AI model's answer to the browser as it is generated.
compare: Compare polling, Server-Sent Events and WebSockets for pushing updates to a browser.
core: Streaming sends a response in pieces as data becomes available instead of waiting for the whole result. Server-Sent Events keep an HTTP response open for one-way server-to-client messages. WebSockets upgrade a connection into a persistent two-way channel.
example: A chat assistant receives tokens from an LLM one at a time. The backend forwards each chunk as an SSE event; the browser's EventSource or a fetch stream reader appends text as it arrives. The user sees the answer forming within a second instead of waiting ten seconds for the full reply.
nuance: Streaming improves perceived latency, not total generation time. Proxies and servers may buffer output unless configured not to. Long-lived connections consume server resources and need timeouts, heartbeats and reconnection. Errors can occur midway after a 200 status was already sent, so the stream needs its own error signal.

concepts.name: Polling
concepts.reference: Short polling repeats requests on an interval; long polling holds a request open until data arrives or a timeout passes. Polling is simple and works through most infrastructure but adds latency, repeated overhead, or both.
concepts.check: Why does short polling waste work when updates are rare?
concepts.bridge: Plain HTTP is request-response: the server cannot speak until the client asks. Polling is the simplest workaround.

concepts.name: Server-Sent Events
concepts.reference: SSE uses a normal HTTP response with content type text/event-stream. The server writes events as text lines; the browser's EventSource parses them and reconnects automatically, optionally resuming with Last-Event-ID. It is one-way, server to client.
concepts.check: Why is SSE often enough for streaming model output?
concepts.bridge: Token streaming only needs the server to keep talking after one request. SSE adds that without a new protocol.

concepts.name: WebSockets
concepts.reference: A WebSocket starts as an HTTP request that upgrades to a persistent, full-duplex connection. Either side can send messages at any time. It suits chat, collaboration and games, but requires custom message formats, reconnection logic and infrastructure that supports upgrades.
concepts.check: When would two-way messaging justify WebSockets over SSE?
concepts.bridge: Some apps need both sides to send freely, such as live collaboration. That calls for a channel rather than a single response.

concepts.name: Buffering and failure handling
concepts.reference: Reverse proxies, compression and frameworks can buffer output and defeat streaming unless flushing is enabled. Idle connections may be closed, so heartbeats help. Because the status code is sent first, mid-stream failures must be reported as an in-band error event.
concepts.check: How should a client learn that generation failed halfway through a stream?
concepts.bridge: A stream passes through many layers between server and browser, and any of them can hold data back or drop the connection.

background: Language models generate text gradually, and users dislike staring at a spinner. Streaming lets the interface show partial results immediately, but it changes how servers, proxies and clients must handle connections.
practice: AI chat backends commonly stream model tokens with SSE or chunked HTTP responses, sometimes relaying through a middle layer to the client. Engineers disable proxy buffering, send heartbeats, handle client disconnects by cancelling generation, and emit a final event marking completion or failure. WebSockets appear when the client must also send messages continuously.

title: API design and versioning
prompt: What makes an HTTP API well designed, and how do you change it without breaking existing clients?
compare: Compare URL versioning, such as /v2/orders, with evolving one API through additive, backward-compatible changes.
core: A well-designed API models resources clearly, behaves consistently, reports errors usefully, and evolves without breaking clients. Once others depend on an API, its request and response shapes become a contract.
example: An orders API exposes GET /orders?cursor=abc&limit=50 returning items plus a next cursor. Errors use a consistent JSON body with a type, message and field details. Adding an optional field is safe; renaming customer_id would break mobile apps that cannot be updated instantly, so it needs a deprecation period or new version.
nuance: Backward compatibility is about client behavior, not just schema: changing defaults, ordering or error codes can break callers. Versioning everything early adds maintenance cost. Mobile apps and third parties keep old versions alive for a long time, so removal requires measured usage and communication.

concepts.name: Resource modeling and consistency
concepts.reference: Model nouns as resources with stable identifiers and use HTTP methods with their usual meanings: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH updates, DELETE removes. Consistent naming, status codes and field formats reduce surprises for clients.
concepts.check: Why should GET requests never change server state?
concepts.bridge: Clients learn an API's patterns once. Consistency lets them predict new endpoints instead of reading special cases.

concepts.name: Pagination and filtering
concepts.reference: Large collections are returned in pages. Offset pagination is simple but can skip or repeat items when data changes and gets slower deep into a table. Cursor pagination uses an opaque position marker and stays stable and efficient.
concepts.check: Why can offset pagination show a duplicate item when new rows are inserted?
concepts.bridge: Returning every row at once is slow and fragile, so APIs hand out results in manageable pieces.

concepts.name: Error responses
concepts.reference: Errors should use accurate status codes and a consistent machine-readable body. RFC 9457 Problem Details defines a standard JSON shape with type, title, status and detail. Validation errors should identify the offending fields without leaking internal details.
concepts.check: What should a client be able to do with a good error response?
concepts.bridge: Clients need to tell a bad input from a missing record from a server failure, and react differently to each.

concepts.name: Compatibility and versioning
concepts.reference: Additive changes, such as new optional fields or endpoints, are usually backward compatible if clients ignore unknown fields. Removing or renaming fields, changing types, or tightening validation are breaking. Breaking changes need a new version, deprecation notices and a migration window.
concepts.check: Why is adding a new required request field a breaking change?
concepts.bridge: You control the server, but not when clients update. Compatibility rules protect callers running old code.

sources.title: RFC 9457: Problem Details for HTTP APIs

background: Backend services are consumed by web apps, mobile apps, scripts and other teams. A clear, stable API lets those clients be built independently; a careless change can break software you never see.
practice: Teams document APIs with OpenAPI, generate typed clients, and review changes for compatibility. Frameworks such as FastAPI derive schemas from code. Mobile backends keep older behavior until usage of old app versions drops. Contract tests and deprecation headers help catch and communicate breaking changes before clients fail.

title: React rendering and state management
prompt: Explain how React decides what to update on screen when state changes.
compare: Compare storing server data in local component state with using a server-state library such as TanStack Query.
core: A React component is a function of props and state that returns a description of the UI. When state changes, React re-renders affected components, compares the new output with the previous one, and commits only the necessary changes to the DOM or native views.
example: A todo list keeps its items in state. Checking one item calls setItems with a new array. React re-renders the list component, reconciles its children by key, and updates only the changed checkbox in the DOM rather than rebuilding the page.
nuance: A re-render is not a DOM update; rendering is calculating, committing is changing the screen. Mutating state in place can prevent updates. Memoization has costs and is not needed everywhere. Many effects are unnecessary: derived values can be computed during render, and server data has caching concerns that plain state does not handle.

concepts.name: Render and commit
concepts.reference: React rendering calls components to produce a new element tree. Reconciliation compares it with the previous tree, using keys to match list items. The commit phase applies the differences to the host environment, such as the browser DOM.
concepts.check: Why do stable keys matter when rendering a reordered list?
concepts.bridge: React separates figuring out what the UI should look like from actually changing the screen.

concepts.name: State, props and immutability
concepts.reference: Props are inputs passed from a parent; state is data a component owns and updates with a setter. React compares state by reference, so updates should create new objects or arrays rather than mutate existing ones. State updates are scheduled, not immediate.
concepts.check: Why might pushing onto an existing state array fail to update the screen?
concepts.bridge: React needs to notice that data changed. Replacing a value is a clear signal; editing it in place is not.

concepts.name: Effects and memoization
concepts.reference: Effects synchronize a component with external systems, such as subscriptions or network calls, after commit. Values derivable from props or state should be computed during render instead. useMemo, useCallback and memo skip work when inputs are unchanged, trading memory and complexity for speed.
concepts.check: When is an effect the wrong tool for computing a value?
concepts.bridge: Effects step outside React's render model, so overusing them adds extra renders and bugs.

concepts.name: Client state versus server state
concepts.reference: Client state, such as an open menu, lives in the app. Server state is a cached copy of remote data that can go stale. Libraries such as TanStack Query handle fetching, caching, deduplication, background refetching and invalidation; stores such as Zustand suit shared client state.
concepts.check: What problems appear when every component fetches the same data into its own state?
concepts.bridge: Data from an API belongs to the server. The UI holds a copy that must be refreshed, shared and invalidated.

sources.title: React: You might not need an effect

background: Interactive interfaces change constantly as users click and data arrives. React lets you describe what the UI should look like for given data and handles updating the screen, but you still need to understand when and why it re-renders.
practice: React and React Native apps typically combine local state for UI details, a small store for shared client state, and a server-state library for API data. Engineers use the React DevTools profiler to find slow renders before adding memoization, keep list keys stable, and invalidate cached queries after mutations.

title: Web accessibility
prompt: What does it mean for a web or mobile app to be accessible, and how do you build one?
compare: Compare using a native HTML button with a clickable div styled to look like a button.
core: Accessibility means people with disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate and operate an interface. It covers screen reader users, keyboard-only users, people with low vision or color blindness, and people with motor or cognitive impairments.
example: A form uses real label elements tied to each input, so a screen reader announces 'Email, edit text.' The submit control is a button element, so it is focusable and works with Enter and Space. Error messages are text, not just red borders, and keyboard focus moves visibly through the fields in order.
nuance: Accessibility is not a final checklist pass; retrofitting is harder than building it in. Automated tools catch only some issues, so manual keyboard and screen reader testing matters. ARIA can fix semantics but misuse makes things worse; native elements are preferred. Accessible design often helps everyone, including older users and people on small screens.

concepts.name: WCAG principles
concepts.reference: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines organize requirements under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable and robust. Success criteria have conformance levels A, AA and AAA; AA is a common legal and organizational target.
concepts.check: Give an example of a requirement under the 'perceivable' principle.
concepts.bridge: WCAG is the widely used standard for accessibility, giving teams testable criteria instead of vague intentions.

concepts.name: Semantic HTML and ARIA
concepts.reference: Native elements such as button, a, label, nav and headings expose roles, names and states to assistive technology automatically. ARIA attributes can add or override semantics for custom widgets, but they do not add keyboard behavior. The first rule of ARIA is to prefer native elements.
concepts.check: Why does adding role='button' to a div not make it fully equivalent to a button?
concepts.bridge: Screen readers read the structure the browser exposes, not the visual styling. Semantics tell them what each element is.

concepts.name: Keyboard and focus
concepts.reference: Every interactive element must be reachable and usable by keyboard, with a visible focus indicator and a logical order. Dialogs should move focus inside, keep it there while open, and return it afterwards. Removing focus outlines without a replacement breaks navigation.
concepts.check: What should happen to keyboard focus when a modal dialog closes?
concepts.bridge: Many users never touch a mouse. Focus shows where their keystrokes will go.

concepts.name: Contrast, text and motion
concepts.reference: WCAG AA requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Information must not rely on color alone. Text should resize without loss of content, and users who prefer reduced motion should not be forced through animations.
concepts.check: Why is a red border alone insufficient to signal a form error?
concepts.bridge: Visual design choices determine whether people with low vision, color blindness or motion sensitivity can use the interface.

sources.title: W3C WAI: ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

background: Many users rely on screen readers, keyboards, magnification or larger text. If an interface only works with a mouse and good eyesight, it excludes them, and public institutions often have legal accessibility obligations.
practice: Teams build with semantic components, test with keyboard only, and check pages with automated tools such as axe or Lighthouse. They also try VoiceOver, TalkBack or NVDA on key flows. React Native exposes accessibilityLabel and accessibilityRole props. Universities and health organizations commonly target WCAG 2.1 or 2.2 AA.

title: Cross-platform mobile with React Native
prompt: Explain how React Native lets one codebase produce iOS and Android apps, and what its limits are.
compare: Compare React Native with building separate native apps in Swift and Kotlin.
core: React Native runs application logic in JavaScript and renders real native UI components rather than a web view. Developers write React components once, and the framework maps them to platform views on iOS and Android, with native modules for device features.
example: A health app shows a goal list, sends local notifications and draws charts. The screens are React components rendered as native views. Notifications use a native module exposed to JavaScript. One TypeScript codebase ships to both the App Store and Play Store, with occasional platform-specific code for differences.
nuance: Cross-platform does not mean zero native work: builds, permissions, signing and some libraries are platform-specific. Upgrades across major versions can be substantial. Performance is usually good, but heavy work on the JavaScript thread can cause jank. Over-the-air updates can change JavaScript but not native code, and must respect store policies.

concepts.name: JavaScript and native layers
concepts.reference: Application code runs in a JavaScript engine, typically Hermes. React describes the UI, and the renderer creates and updates native platform views. The New Architecture replaces the asynchronous bridge with JSI, enabling direct calls between JavaScript and native code, with the Fabric renderer and TurboModules.
concepts.check: What did JSI change compared with the old bridge?
concepts.bridge: Two worlds cooperate: JavaScript holds app logic, while the operating system draws real buttons and lists.

concepts.name: Native modules and platform code
concepts.reference: Device features such as the camera, notifications or secure storage are exposed through native modules written in Swift, Objective-C, Kotlin or Java. Platform-specific files or Platform checks handle differences. Some features require native configuration and permissions.
concepts.check: Why might adding a library require a new native build rather than a JavaScript reload?
concepts.bridge: JavaScript cannot touch phone hardware directly. Native modules are the doorway to platform APIs.

concepts.name: Expo and tooling
concepts.reference: Expo is a framework and toolset around React Native. It provides SDK modules, development builds, config plugins for native settings, and cloud build and submit services. SDK versions are tied to specific React Native versions, so upgrades move together.
concepts.check: What does a config plugin let you change without editing native projects by hand?
concepts.bridge: Plain React Native leaves much native setup to you. Expo packages common needs and build tooling.

concepts.name: Builds and releases
concepts.reference: Apps are compiled, signed and submitted through App Store Connect, often via TestFlight, and Google Play tracks. Store review applies. Over-the-air updates can deliver JavaScript and asset changes to compatible builds, but native changes require a new store release.
concepts.check: Which kinds of fixes can an over-the-air update deliver, and which cannot?
concepts.bridge: Unlike a website, a mobile app lives on the user's device, so shipping changes goes through stores and versioned builds.

sources.title: React Native: About the New Architecture

background: Building separate iOS and Android apps doubles much of the work. React Native lets a team, or a single developer, share most code across platforms while still producing apps that use native interface components.
practice: Teams use Expo or bare React Native with TypeScript, a navigation library, and a server-state library for API data. They test on real devices, manage signing credentials carefully, release through TestFlight and Play testing tracks, and plan SDK upgrades as projects because native dependencies must move in step.

title: TypeScript's type system
prompt: What does TypeScript add to JavaScript, and what does it not protect you from?
compare: Compare TypeScript's compile-time checks with runtime validation of data from an API.
core: TypeScript adds static types to JavaScript. The compiler checks that values are used consistently with their declared or inferred types, then emits plain JavaScript with the types removed. It catches many mistakes before code runs and improves editor tooling.
example: A function expects a User with an id number and an optional email. Calling user.email.toLowerCase() fails type checking because email might be undefined; the developer adds a check. But if an API actually returns id as a string, TypeScript will not notice at runtime unless the response is validated.
nuance: Types are erased at runtime, so they cannot validate external input on their own. The any type disables checking, and type assertions can lie. TypeScript uses structural typing, so unrelated types with the same shape are compatible. Strict mode catches much more than the defaults.

concepts.name: Static checking and erasure
concepts.reference: TypeScript checks types at compile time and removes them in the emitted JavaScript. Inference fills in many types automatically. Runtime behavior is the same as the JavaScript produced, so data crossing a trust boundary still needs runtime validation, for example with a schema library such as Zod.
concepts.check: Why can a correctly typed program still crash on a malformed API response?
concepts.bridge: Static means checked before running. The browser or Node only ever runs JavaScript, never the types.

concepts.name: Structural typing
concepts.reference: TypeScript compares types by their members rather than by declared names. An object is assignable to a type if it has the required properties with compatible types. This fits JavaScript's object style but differs from nominal languages such as Java.
concepts.check: If two interfaces have identical fields, can a value of one be used as the other?
concepts.bridge: Some languages ask what a type is called. TypeScript asks what shape a value has.

concepts.name: Unions and narrowing
concepts.reference: A union type allows several possibilities, such as string | undefined. Checks like typeof, equality, the in operator, or a shared discriminant field narrow the type within a branch. Discriminated unions model states such as loading, success and error safely.
concepts.check: How does a discriminant field help the compiler know which properties exist?
concepts.bridge: Real data often has several valid forms. Narrowing lets the compiler follow your checks and know which form you have.

concepts.name: Generics
concepts.reference: Generics let functions and types work over a type parameter while preserving relationships, such as a function returning the same type it receives. Constraints restrict which types are allowed. They avoid both duplication and the loss of safety from any.
concepts.check: What is lost if a reusable function accepts and returns any instead of a generic type?
concepts.bridge: Reusable code should not forget what kind of data passed through it. Generics carry that information along.

background: JavaScript lets any variable hold any value, which makes large codebases fragile. TypeScript adds a type checker so mistakes such as misspelled properties or missing null checks appear in the editor instead of in production.
practice: Most React and React Native projects now use TypeScript in strict mode. Teams type API responses, often generating types from an OpenAPI schema, and validate untrusted input at runtime. They avoid any, prefer discriminated unions for UI states, and treat type errors as build failures in CI.

title: Front-end performance
prompt: A web page feels slow. How would you measure the problem and improve it?
compare: Compare lab measurements from a tool like Lighthouse with field data from real users.
core: Front-end performance is how quickly a page shows useful content, responds to input and stays visually stable. Core Web Vitals measure these as Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint and Cumulative Layout Shift.
example: A product page loads a 2 MB JavaScript bundle and a large uncompressed hero image. LCP is slow because the image downloads late; clicks feel sluggish because the main thread is busy parsing scripts. Serving a resized modern image, preloading it, and code-splitting rarely used components improves both metrics.
nuance: A fast developer laptop hides problems that mid-range phones on slow networks expose. Lab scores are diagnostic, while real-user field data shows actual experience. Optimizing one metric can hurt another; lazy loading the main image can worsen LCP. Measure before and after rather than applying every tip.

concepts.name: Core Web Vitals
concepts.reference: LCP measures when the largest visible content element renders; good is within 2.5 seconds. INP measures responsiveness to interactions; good is 200 milliseconds or less. CLS measures unexpected layout movement; good is 0.1 or less. Each is assessed at the 75th percentile of page loads.
concepts.check: Which metric captures a button that takes half a second to respond?
concepts.bridge: Speed has several dimensions: seeing content, being able to interact, and the page not jumping around.

concepts.name: JavaScript cost and the main thread
concepts.reference: JavaScript must be downloaded, parsed and executed, mostly on the main thread that also handles input. Large bundles and long tasks delay interactivity. Code splitting, removing unused dependencies and deferring non-critical scripts reduce that cost.
concepts.check: Why can a page look loaded but still ignore taps?
concepts.bridge: The browser's main thread does one thing at a time. While it runs a long script, it cannot respond to the user.

concepts.name: Images, fonts and loading order
concepts.reference: Images are often the largest bytes. Correct sizing, modern formats, compression and responsive srcset reduce them. Explicit width and height prevent layout shift. Prioritizing the main image and deferring offscreen images improves LCP; font loading strategies avoid invisible or shifting text.
concepts.check: How do declared image dimensions reduce layout shift?
concepts.bridge: What the browser downloads first, and how big it is, largely decides what the user sees first.

concepts.name: Lab and field measurement
concepts.reference: Lab tools such as Lighthouse and browser performance panels run controlled tests useful for debugging. Field data, from real-user monitoring or the Chrome User Experience Report, reflects actual devices and networks. Decisions should rest on field data and be verified after changes.
concepts.check: Why might a page score well in Lighthouse but still fail Core Web Vitals in the field?
concepts.bridge: A test on one machine is not your users. Real users bring slower devices, networks and different behavior.

background: Users abandon slow pages, and many browse on mid-range phones and unreliable networks. Performance is measurable, and a few specific metrics capture most of what people experience as speed.
practice: Teams track Core Web Vitals from real users, set bundle-size budgets in CI, and profile slow interactions in browser developer tools. Frameworks such as Next.js and Astro help with code splitting, image optimization and shipping less JavaScript. Changes are compared against field data before and after deployment.

title: Async programming and the event loop
prompt: Explain how async/await lets one thread handle many requests at once.
compare: Compare concurrency with parallelism. Which one does async code provide?
core: Asynchronous programming lets a program start a slow operation, such as a network call, and do other work while waiting. An event loop runs ready tasks and resumes paused ones when their awaited results arrive, so one thread can interleave many I/O-bound tasks.
example: A FastAPI endpoint awaits a database query and an LLM API call. While one request waits on the network, the event loop runs other requests. If the handler instead calls a blocking library like time.sleep or a synchronous HTTP client, the whole loop stalls and every request waits.
nuance: Async helps I/O-bound work, not CPU-bound work; heavy computation still blocks the loop and needs threads or processes. Async is concurrency, not parallelism, on a single thread. Forgetting to await, or mixing blocking calls into async code, causes subtle bugs. Async adds complexity that simple scripts may not need.

concepts.name: The event loop
concepts.reference: The event loop repeatedly takes ready tasks or callbacks from queues and runs them to their next pause point. In JavaScript, promises resolve via the microtask queue, which runs before the next task. In Python, asyncio schedules coroutines and resumes them when awaited futures complete.
concepts.check: What happens to other tasks while one task runs a long loop without awaiting?
concepts.bridge: The event loop is a scheduler on one thread, switching between tasks only at points where they wait.

concepts.name: async and await
concepts.reference: An async function returns a promise or coroutine. await pauses that function until the awaited operation completes, yielding control to the loop meanwhile. Starting several operations before awaiting them, with Promise.all or asyncio.gather, runs them concurrently.
concepts.check: Why are two sequential awaits slower than gathering both operations?
concepts.bridge: await marks a spot where the function steps aside, letting other work proceed until its result is ready.

concepts.name: Concurrency versus parallelism
concepts.reference: Concurrency means multiple tasks make progress over overlapping time, possibly by interleaving. Parallelism means tasks run at the same instant on multiple cores. Async I/O gives concurrency on one thread; CPU-heavy work needs threads, processes or worker pools for parallelism.
concepts.check: Why does async not speed up resizing a thousand images?
concepts.bridge: Juggling several tasks is different from having several hands. Async juggles; multiple cores add hands.

concepts.name: Blocking calls in async code
concepts.reference: A blocking call, such as synchronous file or network I/O or a CPU-heavy function, holds the event loop thread. Use async-native libraries or offload blocking work to a thread or process pool. FastAPI runs plain def endpoints in a threadpool, but blocking calls inside async def endpoints block the loop.
concepts.check: How can one blocking call inside an async endpoint slow down unrelated requests?
concepts.bridge: Async only works if every task cooperates by pausing while it waits. One task that refuses to pause stalls everyone.

background: Web servers spend most of their time waiting on databases, APIs and disks. Async programming lets one process keep serving other users during those waits instead of dedicating a blocked thread to each request.
practice: Node.js and Python frameworks like FastAPI rely on event loops. Engineers use async database drivers and HTTP clients, gather independent calls, set timeouts on every await, and move CPU-heavy work such as embedding large batches to workers. Profiling for a blocked event loop is a common step when latency spikes under load.

title: Big-O and algorithm complexity
prompt: What does Big-O notation tell you about an algorithm, and what does it leave out?
compare: Compare an O(n log n) sort with an O(n squared) sort for ten items versus ten million items.
core: Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's running time or memory grows as input size grows, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms. It lets you compare approaches by how they scale rather than by timing on one machine.
example: Checking whether any two of n users share an email by comparing every pair is O(n squared): doubling users roughly quadruples the work. Inserting each email into a hash set and checking for repeats is expected O(n), using O(n) extra memory. At a million users, the difference is enormous.
nuance: Big-O is an upper bound on growth, not a runtime in seconds. Constants and memory access patterns matter for real input sizes, so an O(n log n) algorithm can lose to a simpler one on small inputs. Worst, average and amortized cases can differ. Space complexity is a separate trade-off from time.

concepts.name: Growth rates
concepts.reference: Common classes, from slower to faster growth, are O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n squared) and O(2 to the n). Big-O keeps the dominant term and drops constants, so 3n plus 20 is O(n). Growth class dominates once inputs are large enough.
concepts.check: Why is 100n considered better than n squared for large n, even though it looks bigger for small n?
concepts.bridge: Big-O asks how work changes as input grows, not how long one run takes.

concepts.name: Worst, average and amortized cost
concepts.reference: Worst-case cost bounds the most expensive input. Average or expected cost assumes an input distribution or randomness. Amortized cost averages over a sequence of operations, such as dynamic array appends that occasionally resize but are O(1) amortized.
concepts.check: How can an append be O(1) amortized when some appends copy the whole array?
concepts.bridge: One algorithm can be fast on typical inputs and slow on unlucky ones, so we say which case we mean.

concepts.name: Time versus space
concepts.reference: Space complexity measures extra memory as input grows. Many speedups trade memory for time, such as caching results or building an index. Recursion uses stack space proportional to depth.
concepts.check: What memory cost does the hash set approach to duplicate detection add?
concepts.bridge: Faster often means remembering more. Memory is a resource with its own limits.

concepts.name: Limits of Big-O in practice
concepts.reference: Asymptotic analysis ignores constant factors, cache behavior, I/O and real input sizes. For small n, simpler algorithms may be faster; insertion sort is used inside some hybrid sorts for small ranges. Profiling confirms where time actually goes.
concepts.check: When might you choose an algorithm with worse Big-O?
concepts.bridge: Big-O guides design, but measured performance on real data settles practical decisions.

sources.title: Python wiki: Time complexity of built-in operations

background: Code that works on a test file can collapse on production data. Big-O gives a shared vocabulary for predicting how an approach scales before you run it at full size.
practice: Engineers use complexity reasoning when choosing data structures, such as a dict or set for membership checks instead of scanning a list, and when spotting nested loops over large collections or N+1 database queries. Interviews often ask for the Big-O of a solution, but production decisions also rely on profiling real workloads.

title: Graphs, BFS and DFS
prompt: Explain breadth-first and depth-first search and give a practical use for each.
compare: Compare storing a graph as an adjacency list versus an adjacency matrix.
core: A graph is a set of nodes connected by edges, which may be directed or weighted. Breadth-first search explores neighbors level by level using a queue; depth-first search follows one path as far as possible before backtracking, using a stack or recursion.
example: In a social network, BFS from one user finds everyone within two connections and the fewest hops to any user. In a build system, DFS over package dependencies detects cycles and produces a topological order so each package builds after its dependencies.
nuance: BFS finds shortest paths only when every edge has equal weight; weighted graphs need algorithms such as Dijkstra's. Both traversals must track visited nodes or they can loop forever on cycles. Deep recursion in DFS can overflow the call stack. Both run in O(V + E) time with an adjacency list.

concepts.name: Graph representation
concepts.reference: An adjacency list stores each node's neighbors and uses O(V + E) space, suiting sparse graphs. An adjacency matrix uses V by V entries, O(V squared) space, and gives constant-time edge checks, suiting dense graphs.
concepts.check: Why is a matrix wasteful for a road network?
concepts.bridge: Nodes are things and edges are relationships, such as people and friendships or tasks and dependencies.

concepts.name: Breadth-first search
concepts.reference: BFS starts at a source, visits all neighbors, then their neighbors, using a FIFO queue and a visited set. It finds the minimum number of edges from the source to every reachable node in an unweighted graph.
concepts.check: Why does using a queue guarantee BFS reaches closer nodes first?
concepts.bridge: BFS spreads outward like ripples, finishing every distance-one node before any distance-two node.

concepts.name: Depth-first search
concepts.reference: DFS explores along a path until it cannot continue, then backtracks. It can be written recursively or with an explicit stack. DFS underlies cycle detection, connected components and finding paths in mazes or dependency trees.
concepts.check: What could happen if DFS did not record visited nodes?
concepts.bridge: DFS commits to one direction and only turns back at dead ends, like exploring a maze by keeping one hand on the wall.

concepts.name: Cycles and topological order
concepts.reference: A directed acyclic graph has a topological order in which every edge goes from earlier to later. It can be computed by DFS finishing order or by Kahn's algorithm, which repeatedly removes nodes with no incoming edges. A cycle means no valid order exists.
concepts.check: Why can a package manager not install two packages that depend on each other in a strict order?
concepts.bridge: Many tasks have prerequisites. A topological order is a schedule that respects them all.

background: Many real problems are about connections: networks, maps, dependencies, workflows and links between documents. Graphs model those connections, and BFS and DFS are the basic ways to explore them.
practice: Graph traversal appears in dependency resolution, build and workflow orchestration, permission hierarchies, recommendation features and agent workflows defined as graphs, such as LangGraph. Engineers usually use adjacency lists, track visited nodes, and choose iterative DFS when graphs can be deep enough to overflow recursion.

title: React hooks
prompt: Explain what React hooks are and how useState and useEffect work, with a practical example.
compare: Compare computing a value during render with storing it in state and updating it from an effect.
core: Hooks are functions that let a function component keep state, refer to values across renders, and synchronize with systems outside React. React relies on hooks being called in the same order on every render.
example: A chat screen uses useState for the draft message, a useRef for the scroll container, and a useEffect that subscribes to a connection when the room ID changes and unsubscribes in its cleanup. The unread count is computed from the message list during render rather than copied into separate state.
nuance: useEffect is not a general-purpose place for logic that runs after a state change; derived values and event responses usually belong in render or event handlers. A missing dependency causes stale values, while suppressing the linter hides the bug. In development, Strict Mode runs effects an extra time to expose missing cleanup.

concepts.name: State with useState
concepts.reference: useState returns the current value and a setter. Calling the setter schedules a re-render with the new value; the variable in the current render does not change. When the next value depends on the previous one, pass an updater function. Objects and arrays should be replaced rather than mutated so React can detect the change.
concepts.check: Why might calling setCount(count + 1) twice in one handler only increase the count by one?
concepts.bridge: State is data a component remembers between renders. Changing it tells React the screen may need to be drawn again.

concepts.name: Effects, dependencies and cleanup
concepts.reference: useEffect runs after React commits a render, to synchronize with something outside React such as a subscription, timer or browser API. The dependency array lists reactive values the effect reads; the effect re-runs when one changes. The returned cleanup function runs before the next run and when the component unmounts.
concepts.check: What could go wrong if an effect subscribes to an event source but returns no cleanup?
concepts.bridge: An external system is anything React does not control, like a network connection or a timer. An effect keeps it in step with the component.

concepts.name: Refs with useRef
concepts.reference: useRef returns a mutable object whose current property persists across renders. Changing ref.current does not trigger a re-render. Refs commonly hold DOM elements, timer IDs or values needed by callbacks without being displayed. Reading or writing refs during render makes output harder to predict.
concepts.check: When would you choose a ref instead of state to store a value?
concepts.bridge: Some values must survive between renders but should not change what is shown, such as an interval ID used later to stop a timer.

concepts.name: Rules of hooks and custom hooks
concepts.reference: Hooks must be called at the top level of a component or custom hook, not inside conditions, loops or nested functions, because React matches hook state by call order. A custom hook is a function starting with use that combines other hooks to share stateful logic. Each component calling it gets its own independent state.
concepts.check: Do two components that call the same custom hook share the same state? Why or why not?
concepts.bridge: React does not label each hook by name; it tracks them by the order they are called during render.

sources.title: React: You Might Not Need an Effect

background: Modern React components are plain functions that run again on every render. Hooks give those functions memory and a controlled way to connect to timers, subscriptions and other systems outside React.
practice: In a React or React Native app, useState holds form input and toggles, useRef holds a list reference or timer ID, and useEffect manages subscriptions such as notification listeners. Custom hooks wrap repeated logic like reading a stored setting. The eslint-plugin-react-hooks rules catch missing dependencies; server data is often better handled by a data-fetching library than by hand-written effects.

title: Middleware in web servers
prompt: Explain what middleware is in a web server and walk through how a request passes through it.
compare: Compare putting an authentication check in middleware with checking it inside each route handler.
core: Middleware is code that runs in a pipeline around request handling. Each layer can inspect or modify the request, end the response early, or pass control to the next layer and act on the response on the way back.
example: An API logs each request, applies CORS headers, parses JSON bodies, and verifies a bearer token before a route runs. If the token is missing, the auth layer returns 401 and the route never executes. On the way out, the logging layer records the status and duration.
nuance: Order matters: a logger registered after an auth layer never sees rejected requests, and body parsing must precede code that reads the body. Middleware is convenient for cross-cutting concerns, but route-specific authorization rules are often clearer as per-route dependencies. Forgetting to call next or return a response leaves a request hanging.

concepts.name: The request-response pipeline
concepts.reference: A framework runs middleware in registration order on the way in. Each layer either passes control onward, as with next() in Express or await call_next(request) in FastAPI, or produces a response itself. Code after passing control runs after inner layers and the handler finish, which allows timing and response headers.
concepts.check: How can one middleware function measure how long the route handler took?
concepts.bridge: Picture layers of an onion: a request travels inward through each layer to the handler, and the response travels back out through the same layers.

concepts.name: Ordering and short-circuiting
concepts.reference: Because layers run in sequence, registration order determines what each layer can see and whether later layers run. A layer can short-circuit by sending a response without passing control, which skips the remaining layers and the route. CORS preflight handling, rate limiting and authentication often short-circuit.
concepts.check: Why should a rate limiter usually run before expensive authentication or database work?
concepts.bridge: Short-circuiting means ending the request early with a response, such as 401 or 429, so nothing further down the chain runs.

concepts.name: Cross-cutting concerns
concepts.reference: Middleware suits behavior that applies to many routes: logging, request IDs, CORS headers, compression, body parsing, authentication and security headers. It can attach data to the request, such as a verified user, for handlers to read. Logic that differs per route is usually clearer in the route or a route-level dependency.
concepts.check: Give one concern that belongs in middleware and one that belongs in a specific route.
concepts.bridge: A cross-cutting concern is a need shared by many routes that would otherwise be copied into every handler.

concepts.name: Error-handling middleware
concepts.reference: Frameworks provide a way to catch errors centrally. Express recognizes error-handling middleware by its four arguments (err, req, res, next) and passes errors to it via next(err); FastAPI uses exception handlers. Central handling gives consistent error responses and avoids leaking stack traces to clients.
concepts.check: Why is it risky to send raw exception messages back to API clients?
concepts.bridge: Without a central handler, each route formats its own errors, and unexpected exceptions may expose internal details or crash the request.

background: Many API routes need the same steps: logging, parsing the body, checking a token, adding headers. Middleware lets a server apply those steps once, in a chain, instead of repeating them inside every route.
practice: In Express, app.use registers middleware such as express.json and a custom token check that sets req.user. In FastAPI, app.add_middleware adds CORS or timing layers, while Depends is often preferred for per-route authentication. In a PHP REST backend, a shared bootstrap that validates a JWT before dispatching to an endpoint plays the same role.

title: CORS and the same-origin policy
prompt: Explain the same-origin policy and how CORS lets a web page call an API on another origin.
compare: Compare a CORS error in a browser with an authentication error from the API.
core: The same-origin policy stops scripts on one origin from reading responses from another. CORS is a set of HTTP headers by which a server tells browsers which other origins may read its responses and with which methods, headers and credentials.
example: A frontend at https://app.example.com calls https://api.example.com with a JSON body and an Authorization header. The browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight. The API replies with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com and the allowed methods and headers, then the browser sends the real request and exposes the response to the script.
nuance: CORS is enforced by browsers, not servers: curl, mobile apps and other servers ignore it, so it is not authorization. A CORS failure often means the request still reached the server; the browser just hid the response. Allowing any origin together with credentials is forbidden, and reflecting arbitrary origins defeats the policy.

concepts.name: Origins and the same-origin policy
concepts.reference: An origin is the combination of scheme, host and port. https://example.com and http://example.com are different origins, as are different ports. By default a script may send some cross-origin requests but cannot read the response unless the server permits it.
concepts.check: Are https://example.com and https://example.com:8443 the same origin?
concepts.bridge: The browser protects data the user is logged in to on one site from being read by scripts on a different site.

concepts.name: Simple requests and preflight
concepts.reference: Requests using non-simple methods such as PUT or DELETE, or headers such as Authorization or a JSON Content-Type, trigger a preflight OPTIONS request. The server answers with Access-Control-Allow-Methods, Access-Control-Allow-Headers and optionally Access-Control-Max-Age. Only if the preflight permits it does the browser send the actual request.
