concepts.check: Why does adding an Authorization header turn a simple request into one that needs a preflight?
concepts.bridge: A preflight is the browser asking permission before sending a request that a server not expecting cross-origin calls might mishandle.

concepts.name: Credentials and allowed origins
concepts.reference: Cookies are sent cross-origin only if the request opts in, for example fetch with credentials: 'include', and the server responds with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. With credentials, Access-Control-Allow-Origin must name the specific origin, not *. Servers should check origins against an allowlist rather than echoing the request's Origin header.
concepts.check: Why is echoing back whatever Origin header arrives a dangerous configuration?
concepts.bridge: Credentials are cookies or HTTP authentication the browser attaches automatically, so allowing them widens what another site can do on the user's behalf.

concepts.name: What CORS does not protect
concepts.reference: CORS controls whether browser scripts can read responses; it does not authenticate callers or stop non-browser clients. Servers must still verify authentication and authorization on every request. CORS also does not prevent all cross-site request forgery, because some cross-origin requests are sent even when the response is unreadable.
concepts.check: If an API has strict CORS settings, can someone still call it from a script on their own machine?
concepts.bridge: CORS is a browser rule that relaxes a browser rule. Anything outside a browser never applies it.

background: When a frontend and an API live on different domains or ports, the browser blocks the page from reading API responses unless the API explicitly allows it. That permission system is CORS, and its errors are among the most common in web development.
practice: FastAPI's CORSMiddleware and the Express cors package set the headers from an allowlist of frontend origins. A dev server on localhost:5173 calling an API on localhost:8000 is cross-origin because the ports differ. React Native apps are not subject to CORS, which is a reminder that the API must enforce its own authentication.

title: Cookies, sessions and JWTs in the browser and apps
prompt: Explain how a web or mobile client should store and send login credentials after a user signs in, and the trade-offs involved.
compare: Compare a server-side session cookie with a JWT access token for keeping a user logged in.
core: After login, the client holds a credential, usually a session ID cookie or a signed token such as a JWT, and presents it on later requests. Where it is stored, how long it lives and how it can be revoked determine much of the application's security.
example: A mobile app completes an OTP login and receives a short-lived JWT access token and a longer-lived refresh token. It keeps both in the platform's secure storage, sends the access token in an Authorization header, and uses the refresh token to get a new access token when an API returns 401 for expiry.
nuance: A standard JWT is signed, not encrypted: anyone holding it can decode its claims, so it must not contain secrets. Stateless tokens cannot be revoked before expiry without extra server state such as a denylist or token versions. HttpOnly cookies resist theft by scripts but bring CSRF concerns; tokens in localStorage avoid CSRF but are readable by any injected script.

concepts.name: Cookie attributes
concepts.reference: HttpOnly prevents JavaScript from reading a cookie, limiting theft through XSS. Secure restricts it to HTTPS. SameSite controls whether it is sent on cross-site requests: Strict, Lax or None, where None requires Secure. Domain, Path and expiry attributes limit where and how long the cookie applies.
concepts.check: What does HttpOnly protect against, and what does it not protect against?
concepts.bridge: Browsers send matching cookies automatically, so attributes decide which requests carry the credential and whether page scripts can see it.

concepts.name: JWT structure and verification
concepts.reference: A JWT has a header, a payload of claims such as sub, exp and iat, and a signature, each base64url-encoded. The server must verify the signature with the expected algorithm and key and check expiry, issuer and audience before trusting claims. Base64 encoding is not encryption.
concepts.check: Why must a server reject a token whose header says the algorithm is none?
concepts.bridge: A JWT is a compact, signed set of statements about the user, so the server can check it without looking up a session record.

concepts.name: Expiry, refresh and revocation
concepts.reference: Short-lived access tokens limit the damage of a leak. A refresh token obtains new access tokens and can be stored server-side, rotated on each use and revoked on logout or suspicion. Without server-side state, a stolen access token stays valid until it expires.
concepts.check: Why pair a short-lived access token with a revocable refresh token rather than issue one long-lived token?
concepts.bridge: Expiry limits how long a stolen credential works; revocation lets the server end access early, which pure stateless tokens cannot do on their own.

concepts.name: Where clients store credentials
concepts.reference: In browsers, HttpOnly Secure cookies keep tokens out of reach of scripts, while localStorage is readable by any script on the origin. Mobile apps should use platform secure storage such as iOS Keychain or Android Keystore-backed storage, for example through Expo SecureStore, rather than plain AsyncStorage.
concepts.check: Why is AsyncStorage a weaker choice than secure storage for a refresh token on a phone?
concepts.bridge: A credential is only as safe as the place it sits; ordinary app or browser storage can be read by code or tools that secure storage blocks.

sources.title: OWASP: JSON Web Token Cheat Sheet

background: Logging in happens once, but every later request must prove who the user is. The app keeps a session cookie or token for that, and choices about storing, expiring and revoking it are a frequent source of security bugs.
practice: A PHP or FastAPI backend might issue JWTs after an OTP check, verifying signature and exp on every endpoint through shared code. A React web app may prefer an HttpOnly SameSite cookie, while an Expo app stores tokens with SecureStore and refreshes on 401. Logging out should revoke the refresh token server-side, not only delete it from the device.

title: Data fetching and caching with TanStack Query
prompt: Explain how a library like TanStack Query manages server data in a React app, and why that is different from storing it in component state.
compare: Compare fetching data in a useEffect and saving it to state with using a query library.
core: Server state is data owned by a backend that the client caches and can go out of date. A query library caches responses by key, tracks loading and error status, deduplicates requests, refetches stale data and updates the cache after mutations.
example: A goals screen calls useQuery with the key ['goals', userId]. Two components using the same key share one request and cache entry. When the user completes a goal, a mutation updates the server and then invalidates ['goals', userId] so the list refetches.
nuance: staleTime and gcTime (formerly cacheTime) are different: stale data can still be shown while refetching, and inactive data is garbage-collected later. Query keys must include every variable the request depends on, or different requests share a cache entry. Optimistic updates need rollback for failures and do not replace server validation.

concepts.name: Query keys and the cache
concepts.reference: Each query is identified by a serializable key, typically an array such as ['todos', { status }]. The cache stores data, status and timestamps per key. Components using the same key share the cached result and in-flight request. Keys should include every parameter the fetch function uses.
concepts.check: What bug appears if a query fetches by page number but the page is missing from its key?
concepts.bridge: A cache needs a name for each stored result. The query key is that name, so two different requests need two different keys.

concepts.name: Stale time and garbage collection
concepts.reference: staleTime sets how long fetched data counts as fresh; the default is zero, so data is stale immediately and may refetch on mount, window focus or reconnect. gcTime sets how long an unused query stays in memory before removal, five minutes by default. Stale data is still returned while a background refetch runs.
concepts.check: If staleTime is zero, will users see a loading spinner every time they revisit a screen? Explain.
concepts.bridge: Fresh means trusted without asking the server again. Unused data is kept a while longer so returning to a screen can show it instantly.

concepts.name: Mutations and invalidation
concepts.reference: useMutation runs create, update or delete requests and exposes their status. After success, invalidateQueries marks related queries stale so active ones refetch, or setQueryData writes a known result directly. Choosing which keys to invalidate keeps the UI consistent with the server.
concepts.check: After adding a new item, why invalidate the list query instead of only appending locally?
concepts.bridge: A mutation changes server data, so cached copies elsewhere in the app may now be wrong and need refreshing.

concepts.name: Optimistic updates and rollback
concepts.reference: An optimistic update changes the cache before the server responds so the UI feels instant. The usual pattern cancels outgoing refetches, snapshots the previous data, writes the expected result, restores the snapshot on error, and invalidates on settle to reconcile with the server.
concepts.check: What should the app do if an optimistic update's request fails?
concepts.bridge: Optimistic means showing the expected result before confirmation, which requires a plan for when the server says no.

background: Data from an API differs from local UI state: other users or devices can change it, it arrives asynchronously, and it can fail or go out of date. Query libraries handle that caching and refetching so components stay simple.
practice: React and React Native apps often pair TanStack Query for server data with a small client store such as Zustand for UI state like selected filters. Engineers set staleTime per query, structure keys by resource and ID, invalidate after mutations, and use optimistic updates for quick actions such as checking off a task. Avoid copying query data into a separate store, which creates two sources of truth.

title: Rendering strategies: CSR, SSR, SSG and hydration
prompt: Explain the difference between client-side rendering, server-side rendering and static site generation, and when you would choose each.
compare: Compare a fully client-rendered single-page app with a statically generated site using interactive islands.
core: Rendering strategy decides where and when HTML is produced: in the browser after JavaScript loads, on a server per request, or once at build time. Each choice trades initial load speed, server cost, freshness of data and interactivity.
example: A nonprofit site's pages rarely change, so they are generated as static HTML at build time and served from a CDN. A donation widget is the only interactive part, so it ships as a small hydrated island while the rest of the page sends no JavaScript.
nuance: Server rendering shows content sooner but does not make a page interactive until its JavaScript loads and hydrates. Static generation is fast and cheap but data is only as fresh as the last build unless pages are rebuilt or revalidated. Hydration mismatches occur when server and client produce different HTML, for example from dates or random values.

concepts.name: Client-side rendering
concepts.reference: In CSR, the server sends a minimal HTML shell and a JavaScript bundle; the browser runs it, fetches data and builds the page. Navigation after load can be fast, but first content waits for the bundle to download and execute. Crawlers and slow devices may see less until scripts run.
concepts.check: Why can a client-rendered app show a blank page on a slow phone even when the server responds quickly?
concepts.bridge: Rendering means turning data and components into the HTML a user sees. In CSR that work happens on the user's device.

concepts.name: Server-side rendering
concepts.reference: In SSR, a server renders HTML for each request using current data, so users see content before client JavaScript runs. It costs server compute per request and adds latency if data fetching is slow. Responses can be cached when content is not user-specific.
concepts.check: What does SSR improve compared with CSR, and what new cost does it add?
concepts.bridge: Doing rendering on the server shifts work from many user devices to infrastructure you operate and pay for.

concepts.name: Static site generation
concepts.reference: SSG renders pages to HTML files at build time. Files can be served from a CDN with no per-request server work, giving fast, reliable delivery. Content changes require a rebuild or an on-demand or incremental regeneration mechanism, so SSG suits content that changes less often than it is read.
concepts.check: Why is SSG a poor fit for a page showing each user's private account balance?
concepts.bridge: Building pages ahead of time works when every visitor should see the same content until the next update.

concepts.name: Hydration and islands
concepts.reference: Hydration attaches event handlers and state to server-produced HTML by running component code in the browser. Hydrating a whole page can be expensive. Islands architecture, used by Astro, ships static HTML by default and hydrates only marked interactive components, controlled by client directives such as client:load or client:visible.
concepts.check: How does hydrating only islands reduce the JavaScript a page needs?
concepts.bridge: Server-rendered HTML looks complete but cannot respond to clicks until JavaScript wires it up; hydration is that wiring step.

background: The same React or Astro components can produce HTML in the browser, on a server for each request, or once when the site is built. That choice affects how quickly pages appear, what hosting costs, and how fresh content is.
practice: A Vite React dashboard behind a login is commonly client-rendered. A content site built with Astro is statically generated and deployed to a CDN such as Cloudflare Pages, with islands only where interaction is needed. Frameworks like Next.js mix strategies per route. Choose based on data freshness, personalization, SEO needs and the JavaScript users must download.

title: CSS layout: flexbox, grid and responsive design
prompt: Explain how flexbox and CSS grid differ, and how you would make a layout work on both phones and wide screens.
compare: Compare flexbox and CSS grid for building a card gallery and a navigation bar.
core: CSS layout places boxes on the page. Every element is a box with content, padding, border and margin. Flexbox arranges items along one axis; grid arranges them in rows and columns at once. Responsive design adapts layout to available space.
example: A header uses flexbox to space a logo and menu across one row and wrap on narrow screens. Below it, a gallery uses grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(16rem, 1fr)) so cards form as many columns as fit, with no breakpoint code for each device size.
nuance: Flexbox can wrap into multiple lines, but each line sizes independently, so items do not align in columns the way grid cells do. box-sizing: border-box changes how width is calculated and avoids many overflow bugs. Media queries respond to the viewport, while container queries respond to a component's own container.

concepts.name: The box model
concepts.reference: Each element's box has content, padding, border and margin. With the default box-sizing: content-box, width sets only the content, so padding and border add to the rendered size. border-box includes padding and border in width. Vertical margins between blocks can collapse into a single margin.
concepts.check: Why can an element set to width: 100% with padding overflow its parent under content-box?
concepts.bridge: Every element occupies a rectangle, and understanding what adds to its size explains most unexpected spacing and overflow.

concepts.name: Flexbox
concepts.reference: Flexbox lays out items along a main axis set by flex-direction, with justify-content aligning along that axis and align-items across it. flex-grow, flex-shrink and flex-basis decide how items share leftover or missing space. The gap property spaces items. It suits toolbars, rows of buttons and centering.
concepts.check: In a row flex container, which property centers items vertically?
concepts.bridge: Flexbox is one-dimensional: it distributes items in a single row or column and lets them stretch or shrink to fit.

concepts.name: CSS grid
concepts.reference: Grid defines rows and columns with grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows, using units such as fr for fractions of free space. Items can span tracks or occupy named areas. repeat with auto-fill or auto-fit and minmax creates responsive columns without media queries. Grid suits page layouts and aligned card galleries.
concepts.check: What does minmax(16rem, 1fr) mean for a column's width?
concepts.bridge: Grid is two-dimensional: rows and columns are defined together, so items line up in both directions.

concepts.name: Responsive design and units
concepts.reference: Responsive layouts use relative units such as rem, percentages and viewport units, flexible tracks, and media queries that change styles at breakpoints. Container queries apply styles based on a parent container's size. The viewport meta tag makes mobile browsers use the device width rather than a zoomed-out desktop width.
concepts.check: When would a container query be more useful than a media query?
concepts.bridge: The same page is viewed on very different widths, so layout should depend on available space rather than one assumed screen.

background: Making a design look right on every screen depends on how CSS sizes and places boxes. Flexbox and grid are the two main modern layout tools, and knowing when to use each removes much trial and error.
practice: Most sites set box-sizing: border-box globally, use flexbox for navigation and button rows, and grid for page regions and card lists. React Native styles use a flexbox model with column as the default direction, so the same concepts transfer to mobile. Test layouts at narrow and wide widths and with larger text settings, not only at one desktop size.

title: Build a task tracker
prompt: How would you build a simple task tracker for a team of five? Scope a first version, choose a data model, trace one action from clicking Add task to the saved task, and say what the user sees if saving fails.
compare: Compare building the first version as one web app with a small database against starting with separate services.
core: A small product is built by scoping a useful first version, choosing a data model that supports it, and making each user action flow clearly from the interface through the server to storage and back.
example: Clicking Add task sends POST /tasks with the title. The server validates it, inserts a row in the tasks table and returns 201 with the saved task, which the list then shows. If saving fails, the typed title stays and an error offers a retry.
nuance: A first version is defined by what it leaves out, not by a smaller copy of everything. SQLite is a reasonable start for one server; a client-server database becomes useful with several app instances or heavy concurrent writes, not merely more users.

concepts.name: Scope a useful first version
concepts.reference: A first version supports the core job end to end: create tasks, mark them done, and see the team's list. Assignment, due dates, notifications and analytics can wait. Stating what is left out, and why, shows judgement about the users' main need.
concepts.check: Which features would you leave out of the first version?
concepts.bridge: Scoping means choosing the smallest feature set that still solves the main problem for the intended users.

concepts.name: Choose a simple data model
concepts.reference: A tasks table needs an id, a title, a completion status and timestamps such as created_at and completed_at; an owner or assignee column links tasks to people. Storing completion time also makes later statistics possible without a separate system.
concepts.check: What would you store for a task, and how would you identify it?
concepts.bridge: A data model decides which facts are stored and how records are identified and related.

concepts.name: Trace one action end to end
concepts.reference: Clicking Add task sends an HTTP request such as POST /tasks with JSON. The backend validates the input, checks the user may create the task, inserts it and returns the created task with a success status. The interface then shows the saved task.
concepts.check: What happens from clicking Add task to seeing the saved task?
concepts.bridge: Tracing one action shows how the interface, the API and the database each take part in a single user step.

concepts.name: Handle failure visibly
concepts.reference: Validation errors return a 4xx status with a message the interface shows next to the input; server or network failures keep the user's typed text and offer a retry. The interface should not show a task as saved until the server confirms it, and repeated clicks should not create duplicates.
concepts.check: What should the user see if saving a task fails?
concepts.bridge: Failure handling decides what the user sees and keeps when a request is rejected or never reaches the server.

background: Building a small application means deciding what it must do first, how its data is stored, and how a user action travels from the screen to the database and back, including what happens when something goes wrong.
practice: Teams usually ship a narrow first version, keep one web app and one database until a real need appears, describe actions as API endpoints, and design error states alongside success states. Validation happens on the server even when the interface also checks input.
